Posted by Richard Cowan on 2004-09-07 16:20:00

Source:

Posted September 7, 2004
Vancouver, BC
Analysis by Richard Cowan Sponsored by Advanced Nutrients.

The City of Vancouver has been presented with the perfect opportunity not only to free itself from the disastrous burdens of cannabis prohibition, but also to reap huge rewards for doing so.

The opportunity began with a sensationalized television news story that pot was being sold openly right here in Rain City. Of course, it was the “openly” part that made it news. Everyone knows that cannabis is almost ubiquitous here, and even though there are many thousands of grow ops, not everyone is growing their own.

Where it was being sold was also a bit of a surprise. It was not on the downtown “Pot-block” popular with tourists, or even in the seedy hard-drug scene just east of there, popular with no one. It was in a very nice little shop on Commercial Drive, in an older, middle-middle class, ethnically mixed neighborhood.

In fact, the Da Kine Smoke and Beverage Shop with its faux-Egyptian motif is a bit nicer than the average. (Commercial Drive would be a good place to learn the meaning of the word “funky,” but there are also lots of good restaurants, casual coffee houses, and gelaterias.)

The owner, Carol Gwilt, also does not fit the stereotype. She is an earnest, middle-age, middle class lady, but no one can say that she does not understand the dangers in hard drugs. Of course, she also understands the dangers in the Drug War, and cannabis prohibition in particular. If I could have asked Central Casting to send us the prefect person for the role, they could not have done any better than Carol.

When she found herself confronted with a CTV (a private Canadian network) television camera in her store, she stood her ground and made very clear that she was fighting a bad law the best way she knew how. The CTV camera crew went next to the police and City Hall. Did they know what was going on??!! The short answer was yes, but they did not like being baited on camera, and they made the inevitable threatening noises.

The next day, the Vancouver Sun quoted a spokesperson for the Commercial Drive merchant association as saying that her group was against Da Kine being there. 

But then something very interesting happened.

The police indicated that they had higher priorities and some City Council members, all of whom are in favor of the legalization of cannabis, said that they thought Da Kine was a good idea. The police said that they would let the city decide, and would just handle it as a “business license” question. (There will be a hearing on September 15th.)

Public opinion

Then the public spoke. Letters to the editors were all supportive. Not surprisingly, it turns out that some of the local restaurant owners really like people with the munchies.

A neighborhood cop said that there were fewer drug dealers in the park where the children play, and there had been no complaints to the police in the four months that it had been open.

Next, CTV sent a hidden camera into an upstairs store on the Pot-Block, where they revealed that marijuana was already being sold! The grainy black and white pictures would have made Mr. Rogers’ neighborhood look sinister, and CTV seemed to be saying, “Had you rather buy weed from these grainy gray figures or the nice lady with the nice store who wants to pay taxes?”

Nonetheless, for the next couple of days, discretion was appropriate. They stopped selling weed to all but a few patients, and asked their customers to fill out forms to join and petitions for the City Council.

In a matter of days, they had thousands! Customers and patients gave interviews on the sidewalk in front of the shop. People here are not afraid to speak out. Unlike the Land of the Police and Home of the No-Knock Raid, the citizens of Vancouver are not intimidated into silence.

On Monday, Labor Day here as in DEAland, the Vancouver Sun reported that marijuana was also being sold across the street at The Spirit Within, which also sells other herbs, as the name implies.

This excerpt from the Sun story sums up the situation:
"Unlike at Da Kine, customers at The Spirit Within are not asked to fill out a form saying they use marijuana for medical purposes.

 Vancouver police spokeswoman Const. Sarah Bloor said she couldn't confirm until members of the drug squad returned from holidays on Tuesday whether the squad was aware that The Spirit Within was openly selling marijuana.

Len Hewer, who described himself as a regular customer of The Spirit Within, said the store usually has about four different varieties of marijuana for sale.

"It's excellent," said Hewer. "I know I'll get an honest weight and an honest price."

Hewer said he wasn't sure how long the store had been open, but said he'd been going there to purchase marijuana for about four months.

Hewer said he takes marijuana for various medical conditions, but said he hasn't received official approval to use the drug from Health Canada.

Possession of a one-month supply of medicinal marijuana is legal in Canada for people who are terminally or chronically ill and have approval from Health Canada to use the drug.
(emphasis added)

While The Spirit Within did a brisk business Sunday, it was not nearly as busy as the Da Kine cafe -- which has been subject to intense media attention since its owner, Carol Gwilt, confirmed last week that she had been selling marijuana since the shop opened four months ago.

Bloor has said police were aware the Da Kine cafe was selling marijuana, but the force did not have the resources to launch an investigation.

She said police expressed their concerns about the cafe to the City of Vancouver's licensing department.

The city will hold a hearing Sept. 15 to determine if Da Kine's business licence should be revoked. However, councillors Tim Louis and Anne Roberts have already said they don't think shutting down the cafe should be a top priority for the city.
See
Exclusive to MarijuanaNews: Vancouver City Council Members Visit New Amsterdam Café. All Smiles and They Weren’t Even Smoking!

Gwilt said Sunday she has not been contacted by police, but refused to comment further, saying she was too busy.

A steady stream of people visited Da Kine Sunday, at the rate of about one a minute.

Brian Feldbloom, who visited the cafe after hearing about it in the news, said he couldn't believe how busy it was.

"It's packed," he said. "They're so busy that they ran out of the cheap stuff."

 As this story makes clear, Da Kine was not really the first place to sell cannabis more or less openly, but it is simply the first public cannabis store. I am sure that the police have known about it, and The Spirit Within, as well as several other places in Vancouver where cannabis has been sold for some time. 

The medical nexus

As the Sun story indicates, Da Kine requires its patrons to fill out a form saying they use marijuana for medical purposes. Actually, the following four categories are eligible for membership:

  1. People with a Health Canada medical exemption.

  2. People with a prescription for marijuana or Marinol from their doctor.

  3. People with a recommendation from a certified Naturopath, Homeopath, or Chiropractor.

  4. People who fill out a sworn affidavit stating “how marijuana benefits their health and well-being.” 

Obviously, one need not be a lawyer to see that the last item offers a rather large loophole, and inevitably raises the question as to whether they are just hiding behind medical use as a way to sell cannabis to non-medical users. And that is just what the prohibitionists claim that the whole marijuana reform movement is doing.

Of course, that is logically irrelevant.

No one who knows Carol Gwilt would ever doubt the sincerity of her belief that cannabis should be legal, but that there should be some provision for sick and dying people to be able to get it until everyone can buy it. In any case, the City of Vancouver cannot formulate its policies based on the sincerity of advocates for various positions.

Nonetheless, the medical issue remains relevant. Almost exactly one year ago, BC Judge Patrick Chen echoed the Parker ruling in Ontario that the Canadian marijuana laws were void because Health Canada had failed to provide a workable method of providing sick and dying Canadians with cannabis.
For an explanation of the Parker ruling see
Canadian Court Says Lack of Provision for Medical Marijuana Violates Fundamental Rights; Gives Parliament 12 Months to Fix Prohibition Laws -- Or Marijuana Possession Is Legal in Largest Province.
and
Is Health Canada’s Medical Marijuana Fiasco A Time Bomb Ticking Under Canadian Prohibition?

Judge Chen wrote, "While I agree that I am not bound by Parker, in my view it should be followed unless there is a good reason not to do so.  It is, after all, a decision of the Ontario Court of Appeal and no decision of this province's court of Appeal has addressed the issue of the constitutionality of section 4's prohibition against marijuana on the basis of medical use."

Subsequently, a ruling by the Ontario courts reinstated the marijuana laws – subject to Health Canada meeting its obligations to cannabis patients. Whether or not they could actually reinstate those laws has been questioned, but the fact remains that Health Canada still has not provided a workable system to take care of the huge need for medical cannabis. (The Canadian Medical Association has estimated that there may be half a million people in Canada who are already using cannabis medically – but illegally.)

Judge Chen’s ruling was not challenged by the Crown so there has been no higher court ruling. Consequently, it applied only in that one case. The point is not that cannabis is legal in BC, but rather that the BC Courts would be very likely to echo the Parker ruling, and would be much less tolerant of Health Canada’s truculence than were the Ontario Courts.

The City Council of Vancouver should consider the following points:

  1. Health Canada is still providing less than one thousand Canadians with exemptions, while Vancouver’s BC Compassion Society has over 2,000 members and cannot accommodate many more members.
    See
    Canadian Health Minister Seeks Asylum In DEAland; Says Making Her Think About Medical Cannabis Constitutes Torture. “In DC They Don’t Allow That Sort of Thing. Thinking, That Is.”

  2. California is providing for many more medical marijuana patients than Canada despite active opposition of the US federal government.
    See
    Blame DEAland: Canadian Health Minister Blames DEA for Canadian Medical Cannabis Fiasco. DEA Wouldn’t Sell Them Seeds. Now If Someone In Canada Would Go Into The Seed Business…

  3. When Health Canada licensed a grower to supply patients with cannabis, it chose a company with no experience with cannabis. Subsequently, the cannabis produced by this company has been rejected by patients who complain about its poor quality.
    See
    Health Canada Gives $5.7 Million Contract to Company With No Experience to Grow Mediocre Weed for Medical Marijuana Research

  4. Similarly, when Health Canada established a “Stakeholders Committee” for medical cannabis, they included numerous police and other prohibitionists, but excluded anyone from the Compassion Societies, the very people with the most direct knowledge about the medical uses of cannabis.
    See
    Health Canada’s “Office of Cannabis Medical Access' Stakeholder Advisory Committee” Includes “Physicians for A Smoke Free Canada” - Not The Compassion Societies. But It Will Let Them Talk… For An Hour

  5. Health Canada has made it unnecessarily difficult for patients to get medical cannabis.

  6. The Canadian Medical Association and its provincial affiliates have discouraged their members from providing their patients with recommendations for medical cannabis.
    See
    Cruelty, Incompetence, And Quackery Threaten Canadian Medical Cannabis Patients.

  7. It is increasingly difficult for Canadians to get a personal physician and even more difficult to get to see a specialist, which is required for patients who are not terminal.

  8. Hard drug addicts who live on the streets or in flop houses are generally unable to get a doctor, but they often have the greatest need for medical cannabis, and need a safe place to smoke it.
    See
    Marijuana Legalization, The Missing Pillar in Solving the Substance Abuse Problem in Vancouver and All of Canada. Analysis By Richard Cowan

  9. Health Canada still denies that cannabis has any medical uses and has blocked the very research which they claim to want.
    See
    Hypocrisy and Democracy: Raid on Medical Cannabis Research Facility Critical of Health Canada’s Schwag Challenges Canada’s Values. What Will The Politicians Say?

In short, there is every reason to conclude that HC is acting in bad faith and the City of Vancouver should not wait on the courts to eliminate the cruel and unjustifiable impediments to medical access to cannabis.

Will healthy people get access to “medical cannabis”?

Until God starts diagnosing patients and writing prescriptions, either sick people are going to be denied needed cannabis or healthy people will get access to it. The real question remains: which is more important, helping the sick and dying or maintaining cannabis prohibition? The evidence is overwhelming that HC has  decided that its priorities lie in maintaining prohibition.
See
Health Canada Press Release Makes Clear that the Health of Canadians Is Less Important than Marijuana Prohibition. Victimization of a Patient Gives More Proof.

This is not the direction that Vancouver has taken. Technically, the BC Compassion Society, which is a dozen blocks up Commercial Drive from Da Kine, is breaking the law when it supplies most of its members, who have been unable to jump through HC’s hoops.
From 1999 see
Canadian Medical Association Journal Carries Favorable Article On Vancouver Compassion Club

Learning Dutch?
From 2000 see
Professor Of Medicine At The University Of Toronto Urges Canada To "Go Dutch" At Vancouver Conference On Health, Addictions And Social Justice.

All of the members of the Vancouver City Council favor the legalization of cannabis, but what can they do about it?
See
Swiss Government Says Going Dutch Does NOT Violate Treaties. Implications for Other Countries, Especially Canada and UK. Plus Full Text of UN Nark Press Release.

It has been almost 30 years since the Dutch decided that cannabis prohibition was counterproductive and started allowing the sale of cannabis in “coffee shops.” This policy has been hugely successful, but it has not been without its problems in the context of international cannabis prohibition.

There were two fundamental reasons that the Dutch cite for their policies. First, they did not like arresting young people for possession of cannabis. Second, they wanted to separate the market for cannabis from hard drugs.

It may come as a surprise that The Netherlands has a lower rate of cannabis use than does Canada – and much lower than either the US or UK.
For an interesting international comparison of cannabis use rates click here

However, it should not come as a surprise that they have a much lower rate of hard drug use than many of the most prohibitionist countries, including Canada.
See
Good News From Holland Is Even Better in Context. “Large Majority” of Dutch Parliament Favors Legalization of Cannabis. Most EU Countries Recognize Dutch Model Superior to DEAland’s. We Are Winning!

That is the real triumph of the Dutch cannabis policies, and the most compelling reason that Vancouver urgently needs its own “coffee shop system.”

It is also worth noting that almost ten years ago some of the cannabis shops started their own medical cannabis (mediwiet) system, providing half-price cannabis to patients, thus reducing the demand for a medical distribution system. When Holland finally established a medical cannabis system, it found it was difficult to compete with the discounted recreational products.
See
Scientific and Ethical Implications of Dutch Medical Cannabis Program for Health Canada. Does Making Cannabis Available By Prescription Before The Research Is Completed Offer A Way Out?

Although there are significant differences between the Canadian and Dutch legal and political systems, in both countries the laws are made nationally but enforced locally. Consequently, Dutch cities control their own cannabis policies. Cannabis remains technically illegal to possess, sell or grow, but cities have their own policies within certain national guidelines, which have evolved over the years. Originally, there were almost no workable rules, but that has changed as the national government reconciled itself to accepting the system. Now there are actual licenses.

There are some basic rules for Dutch coffee shops:

  1. No hard drugs.

  2. No one under 18.

  3. No disturbing the neighbors.

  4. No advertising.

  5. There is now a 5 gram limit per transaction, but it is not aggressively enforced, and it may not be appropriate for Vancouver.

(The rule against hard drugs is the most important. A coffee shop will be closed immediately if it is found selling hard drugs. The age limit used to be 16, but the Dutch raised it under foreign pressure, and have expressed regret for having done so. It is important to note that there are almost never any police calls to coffee shops. Vancouver has had a few years experience with on-premise consumption of cannabis on the Pot Block and a few other places, and there have been no problems. As in Holland, there are thousands of police calls to bars to deal with alcohol related problems. The rule against advertising is interpreted differently in different cities, but generally it means “be discrete.”)
Radio Netherlands has a good description of the coffee shop system

The question coming up on September 15th will simply be whether Vancouver should pull the business license for Da Kine. It is obvious that if they try to close Da Kine it will persevere, and there will continue to be other places where cannabis will be sold – albeit a bit more discretely.

If they decide – as I expect – that closing Da Kine would be bad social policy, then other places will open around the city very quickly. Amsterdam has roughly the same population as Vancouver proper, and has almost 300 coffee shops, but it gets far more tourists than Vancouver.

Haarlem, which gets very few non-Dutch tourists has 16, which is one "coffee shop" per ten thousand population. On that basis, one might expect that Vancouver might have roughly 50 shops. Right now the only problem with Da Kine is that they have too little competition. If they had the only donuts in Vancouver the problems would be the same, or worse (the local restaurants would do less business rather than more.)

The City Council should try an experiment for a year or so. If it doesn’t work out and the sky falls… Well, the crack dealers would be more than happy to provide cannabis again.

Drugs tourism?

One of the sleazier prohibitionist clichés labels (libels?) people who go to Holland to enjoy the freedom to use cannabis as “drug tourists.” Of course, this label is never used for people who go somewhere to drink the local wine. In fact, Vancouver would benefit enormously from having cannabis cafes. It would not only eliminate the problems associated with prohibition and help the sick and dying, it would also bring tens of thousands of affluent American, Canadian, and Asian tourists who are cannabis users. 

The prohibitionists like to paint cannabis users as impoverished “hippies” who have no money to spend on anything else. In fact, cannabis users generally have more education than non-users and consequently have more disposable income than non-users – unless their lives have been wrecked by getting arrested, for their own good, of course.

A coffee shop system here would also be a great boon to the entertainment industry. Vancouver would be even more popular with the movie and music industries. (Rumor has it that some musicians smoke pot.)

Ah, but what would DEAland do? Would Bush pull the troops out of Iraq to invade Canada? Would they close the border and stop Canadians from spending money with American hotels and merchants? Would they stop buying Canadian oil or gas? Would they disrupt US manufacturing which is dependent on Canadian components?
See
DEAland Threats Make The News In Canada, Headlines In Vancouver, But Disrupting Canadian Trade Would Hurt American Companies, So It Is Important That the Threats Not Be Publicized At Home.

The answer seems obvious, but the surest way to shut up the US prohibitionists, and particularly our sociopathic Drug Czar, would be for Vancouver mayor Larry Campbell to challenge John Walters to a debate. That would send Walters running to the Mexican border.

In fact, Campbell should challenge the Canadian Prime Minister to a debate. Canada needs a national debate on cannabis prohibition, because freedom has nothing to fear from the truth – least of all in Vancouver.
